title: Antiderivatives and indefinite integration
section: Indefinite Integration (Antidifferentiation) ▷ Definitions and elementary formulas
terms: antiderivative; indefinite integral; integrand; constant of integration; variable of integra- tion; power integration rule.

exposition.text:

An antiderivative of f on an interval is a differentiable function F with F = f. The notation

f (x) dx = F (x) + C describes all antiderivatives there; any two differ by a constant by the mean
value theorem. The integrand is f (x), and dx identifies the variable. On disconnected domains,
separate components may have different constants.

Riemann integrability alone does not guarantee an antiderivative on the entire interval. A jump
in the integrand can prevent any differentiable primitive from existing across that point, even
though a definite integral is well defined.

question.text:
On R \ {0}, which is the most general antiderivative of 1/x?
(A) log x + C
(B) log |x| + C with one shared constant required
(C) log |x| + C for x > 0 and log |x| + C for x < 0, with independent constants
+ −
2
(D) 1/x + C
(E) No antiderivative exists.

solution.text:
log |x| differentiates to 1/x on each component. The zero-derivative theorem forces con-
stancy on each interval separately, not one common constant across the missing point
zero.

question.text:
′ ′
If F = f on an interval and G = 2f + 3, which expression is constant?
(A) G − F − 3x (B) G − 2F − 3x (C) G − 2F + 3x (D) G − 2F (E) 2G − F

solution.text:
Differentiating the stated expression gives (2f + 3) − 2f − 3 = 0. A differentiable function
with zero derivative on an interval is constant.

question.text:
Let f(x) = 0 for x < 0 and f(x) = 1 for x ≥ 0. Does f have an antiderivative on (−1, 1)?
(A) Yes: max{x, 0}.
(B) Yes: |x|.
(C) Yes, after choosing different integration constants on the two sides.
(D) No, because differentiability at zero cannot be achieved.
(E) No, because f is unbounded.

solution.text:
Any candidate must be constant on (−1, 0) and equal to x plus a constant on (0, 1). Dif-
ferentiability requires continuity at zero, forcing the constants to match, but the resulting
left and right derivatives are 0 and 1. The function is bounded and Riemann integrable, yet
has no antiderivative across its jump.
